catalog_quote: The stress in Shilḥa vernaculars is not phonemic. It is predominantly weak and this confirms Basset's statement ... In monosyllabic and isolated words, the stress falls on the initial vowel, as in [ânu] 'well'; [ûl] 'heart'; [îzi] 'flies'. In polysyllabic words with zero affixes which do not contain a long vowel, the main stress falls on the first syllable as in [tázribt] 'fold'; [táhyaṣt] 'buckle'; [áʕšuš] 'tent'. As for words which contain a long vowel, this vowel usually attracts the stress as in [abrîd] 'road'; [ḥaṣîlu] 'any way'; [magrûn] 'shot gun'; [aqallîli] 'poor'. ... The possessive affixes -inwin, -nikmit, -is are stressed. The stress shifts from the first syllable to the penultimate, as in áʕšuš 'tent', cf. [aʕšušínwin] 'their tent'; [ânu] 'well', cf. [anuníkmit] 'their well'. ... Therefore, the stress patterns of Douiret may be generally summarised as follows: First, in monosyllabic and isolated words, the stress falls always on the first syllable. Second, long vowels seem to always attract stress in Douiret. This rule applies to both nouns and verbs. Third, plural suffixes, enclitics and proclitics may either receive stress or cause stress shift from the first syllable to the affix. (Gabsi 2003: 96-98) ... Long vowels are always stressed regardless of their position in a word. (Appendix VI, p. 384, Ouirsighen)

new_statements.quote: Les noms de parenté munis d'un suffixe pronominal portent l'accent sur la pénultième : mémmis « son fils », yíllis « sa fille » tandis que tous les autres noms le portent sur la dernière syllabe : lqåṣrís « son château », afusýs « sa main ». […] Le locatif est caractérisé par le déplacement de l'accent sur la dernière syllabe : ángu « cuisine », angú « dans la cuisine ». (Notes recueillies sur place en 1974). A l'île de Jerba, à Guellala, l'accent joue un rôle prépondérant et possède également une valeur phonologique. Le locatif est accentué sur la dernière syllabe comme à Tamezreṭ : әlmáγrәb « soir », әlmaγrәb « dans la soirée ».
new_statements.translation: Kinship nouns bearing a pronominal suffix carry the accent on the penult: mémmis 'his son', yíllis 'his daughter', whereas all other nouns carry it on the last syllable: lqåṣrís 'his castle', afusýs 'his hand'. […] The locative is characterised by a shift of the accent to the last syllable: ángu 'kitchen', angú 'in the kitchen'. (Notes collected on the spot in 1974.) On the island of Jerba, at Guellala, the accent plays a preponderant role and also has phonological value. The locative is accented on the last syllable, as at Tamezreṭ: әlmáγrәb 'evening', әlmaγrәb 'in the evening'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent position is morphologically conditioned and contrastive rather than fixed by syllable count: in Tamezreṭ, kinship nouns with a pronominal suffix are stressed on the penult (mémmi-s), all other suffixed nouns on the final syllable (afus-í-s), and the locative is formed by shifting the accent to the final syllable (ángu ~ angú); in Jerba (Guellala) accent is phonological, the locative is final-accented, and definite adjectives shift the accent to the initial (old-article) syllable. Zuwara bare nouns are stressed on the first syllable (áfrux, árgaz, ílis) and on the last stem syllable before a possessive suffix (argáz-is) — i.e. penultimate in both cases. A secondary native-speaker web source (Ben Mamou 2005) says Tamezret accent falls 'often on the penultimate syllable' but depends on context and intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: l'eylt-í-s 'sa femme' takes final accent like ordinary nouns because of its Arabic origin; sídi-s 'son maître' is assimilated to the kinship nouns (penult). Jerba: definite adjective ámәllal 'le blanc' (accent on the old article) vs amәllál 'blanc, un blanc'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent in isolated nouns (bare and with pronominal suffix) and the locative form; for Jerba also short phrases (gárri tíli tamәllalt). Tamezreṭ generalisation is drawn from Stumme's 1900 marked texts plus the author's 1974 field notes; the Jerba data are the author's own (Guellala); the Zwara data (§4: áfrux, árgaz, ílis vs argáz-is, afrúx-is, ilís-is) are second-hand from Mitchell 1953. No general default for unsuffixed Tunisian words is given; Ben Mamou's Tamezret website (2005, saved) says the accent 'se place souvent sur l'avant-dernière syllabe' and depends on context and intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Tamezreṭ (Matmata hills, Tunisia; inside tuni1262 but not a separately coded Glottolog dialect) and Guellala on Jerba (Glottolog dialect jerb1241); §4 of the same entry reports Zuwara, Libya (the 'Zuwara' half of tuni1262) second-hand from Mitchell 1953. Nothing found first-hand for Douiret-Chenini (doui1234), whose description is Gabsi 2003 (inaccessible). Provotelle 1911 (also saved) describes Sened, a separate Glottolog language (sene1271), not this one.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Shilha has an empty rule; the one existing statement (Vycichl & Chaker 1984, read as weight-sensitive) covers only suffixed nouns and the locative in Tamezret and Jerba. Gabsi agrees with that reading in type (weight-sensitive; possessive suffixes -is/-inwin/-nikmit take the stress, matching Vycichl's lqåṣrís, afusýs) and refines it by supplying the default for unsuffixed words (initial unless a long vowel attracts the stress), the treatment of plural suffixes and clitics, the Ouirsighen sentence-final shift, and the statement that stress is not phonemic. It differs from Vycichl on Jerba: Vycichl §10 says the accent at Guellala 'possède également une valeur phonologiq…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic and weak. Default: first syllable (initial vowel) of the word in isolation; a long vowel anywhere in the word attracts the stress instead (nouns and verbs). Suffixes and clitics disturb the default: plural -awin and possessive -inwin/-nikmit/-is are stressed (stress moves from the first syllable to the penultimate, e.g. áʕšuš 'tent' vs. aʕšušínwin 'their tent'); plural -an and verbal enclitics -asin/-ak and the negative proclitic are unstressed. Imperatives stress the first syllable. Appendix VI: same system in Ouirsighen (Jerba) and Chninni; in Ouirsighen a word in sentence-final position shifts its stress to the last syllable (tázaqqa ~ tzaqqá), and verbs with an initial consonant cluster stress the final syllable; in Chninni verbs stress the final syllable after a geminate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A secondary-stress diacritic is defined in footnote 39 (p. 95: 'main stress; secondary stress; stressed long vowel') but no secondary-stress rule is stated in the text.
new_statements.exceptions: Plural -an is not stressed (especially after a long vowel: ábrid/ibrîdan); verbal proclitics (negative) and enclitics -asin, -ak do not take stress in Douiret, whereas in Ouirsighen verb enclitics and the negative -i(š) marker do take stress; Ouirsighen sentence-final stress shift; the analysis of Ouirsighen and Chninni is called 'tentative'. Gabsi p. 99 summary: 'stress falls on the first syllable, penultimate and final syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Gabsi 2003 describes the Douiret vernacular (doui1234, a dialect of tuni1262) in the main text and, in Appendix VI, Chninni (Chenini, doui1234) and Ouirsighen (island of Jerba, jerb1241). 'Shilha' in his title means these southern Tunisian Berber vernaculars collectively, not Tashelhiyt of Morocco. The existing Vycichl 1984 statement concerns Tamezreṭ (Glottolog tame1243, filed under chen1266 Western Algerian Berber, flagged by the second reader) and Guellala on Jerba.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement on phonemic status, not on placement: Vycichl & Chaker 1984 §10 (Guellala, Jerba) state that the accent has phonological value there (determined ámәllal vs. amәllál), while Gabsi 2003 (p. 96 for Douiret; App. VI p. 384 for Ouirsighen on Jerba and for Chninni) states that stress is not phonemic and is weak, with the Ouirsighen/Chninni analysis explicitly labelled tentative. On placement the two sources are compatible: both give a weight- and morphology-conditioned system in which possessive suffixes and the locative pull the stress rightward and, per Gabsi, long vowels attract it while the default is initial. Vycichl's kinship-noun penult rule (mémmis, yíllis) for Tamezret has no counterpart in Gabsi, whose data are from Douiret, Chenini and Jerba; and Glottolog files Tamezret (tame1243) under chen1266 rather than tuni1262, so the Vycichl §9 passage may not even be about this languoid.

sources.note: Tamezreṭ: kinship nouns + pronominal suffix stress the penult (mémmis, yíllis), all other suffixed nouns the final syllable (lqåṣrís, afusýs); locative shifts accent to the final syllable (ángu ~ angú). Jerba/Guellala: accent 'joue un rôle prépondérant' and is phonological; locative final (әlmáγrәb ~ әlmaγrәb); definite adjective ámәllal vs amәllál. Zwara (from Mitchell 1953): áfrux, árgaz, ílis but argáz-is, afrúx-is, ilís-is with possessive suffix.
